Linn) on the damages induced by nicotine in rats as compared to alpha-tocopherol Abstract The beneficial effects of onion oil as an antioxidant has been assessed in nicotine administered rats by studying whether the peroxidative damage caused by nicotine can be effectively combated with the onion oil and the effects compared to vitamin E, a highly efficient antioxidant. Lipid peroxidation products and antioxidant defence system have been studied in liver, lungs, and heart. The rats were injected with nicotine (0.6 mg/kg body wt.) and simultaneously given onion oil (100 mg/kg body wt.) or vitamin E (100 mg/kg body wt.) for 21 days. Concentration of free fatty acids, TBA reactive substances (TBARS), conjugated dienes and hydroperoxides were significantly increased in the tissues of nicotine treated rats as compared to normal rats. Onion oil supplemented to nicotine treated rats showed increased resistance to lipid peroxidation and the effect was near to that of vitamin E fed rats. The activity of catalase and superoxide dismutase decreased in nicotine treated rats. Antioxidants-glutathione content, vitamin C and retinol showed no significant difference but liver vitamin E content significantly decreased in nicotine treated rats. On onion oil or vitamin E supplementation, the concentration of antioxidants were significantly raised in all the tissues studied, however, a significantly increased concentration of glutathione, vitamin E and retinol was noticed in vitamin E+nicotine treated rats. Thus, these results indicate that onion oil is an effective antioxidant against the oxidative damage caused by nicotine as compared to vitamin E. Introduction Nicotine, a major toxic component of cigarette smoke, plays an important role in the development of cardiovascular disease and lung cancer in smokers. Experiments in our laboratory have shown that chronic administration of nicotine alone or in combination with alcohol or high fat diet caused increased lipid levels as well as lipid peroxidation products in serum and tissues of rats (Latha et al., 1993, Ashakumary and Vijayammal, 1996a, Ashakumary and Vijayammal, 1996b, Ashakumary and Vijayammal, 1997). There are reports that nicotine infusion did affect the trace element relationship between tissues as well as components of the free radical defence system (Dubick and Keen, 1991, Bui et al., 1995) and an in vitro model using Chinese ovary cells, also induced oxidative stress (Yildiz et al., 1998). Recent studies in rats showed that nicotine treatment adversely affected the coronary risk profile by increasing blood pressure (Swislocki et al., 1997). Onion (Allium cepa. Linn), one of the important Allium species commonly used in our daily diet have been extensively studied for their therapeutic uses as antibiotic, antidiabetic, antiatherogenic, anticancer etc (Augusti, 1996). Biological action of Allium products is ascribed to organosulfur compounds. Onion oil has been reported to effectively decrease the lipid levels in experimental animals (Bordia et al., 1975, Bordia et al., 1977, Bobbi et al., 1984). It has been found that administration of onion products to diabetic rats significantly reduced hyperglycaemia (Kumud et al., 1990). Antioxidants are of extreme importance as far as oxidative stress induced degenerative diseases are concerned. Vitamin E or α-tocopherol is believed to be one of the principal biological antioxidants against lipid peroxidation (Burton and Traber, 1990, Evstigneeva et al., 1998). A number of studies have demonstrated its protective role against oxygen free radical-mediated lipid peroxidation in tissue injury (Abbey, 1995, Knight, 1998, Neuzil and Baoutina, 1998). Harats et al. (1990) reported that acute smoking exerted an oxidative stress on plasma lipoproteins and that higher plasma levels of natural antioxidants such as vitamins C and E have a protective role. Reports from our laboratory also evidenced that treatment of vitamins C or A protected rats from the deleterious effects caused by cigarette smoke (Helen and Vijayammal, 1997a, Helen and Vijayammal, 1997b). Furthermore, supplementation of diet rich in vitamin C, vitamin E and β-carotene resulted in a highly significant decrease in endogenous oxidative damage in the lymphocyte DNA of both smokers and nonsmokers (Duthie et al., 1996). Since nicotine is a major component of cigarette smoke, we have tried to evaluate whether the supplementation of onion oil has any protective role against nicotine induced lipid peroxidation and antioxidant defence mechanisms in rats and the results have been compared to that of α-tocopherol, a highly efficient antioxidant. Abstract All of the naturally occurring vitamin E forms, as well as those of synthetic all rac-α-tocopherol, have relatively similar antioxidant properties, so why does the body prefer α-tocopherol as its unique form of vitamin E? We propose the hypothesis that all of the observations concerning the in vivo mechanism of action of α-tocopherol result from its role as a potent lipid soluble antioxidant. The purpose of this review then is to describe the evidence for α-tocopherol’s in vivo function and to make the claim that α-tocopherol’s major vitamin function, if not only function, is that of a peroxyl radical scavenger. The importance of this function is to maintain the integrity of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in the membranes of cells and thus maintain their bioactivity. That is to say that these bioactive lipids are important signaling molecules and that changes in their amounts, or in their loss due to oxidation, are the key cellular events that are responded to by cells. The various signaling pathways that have been described by others to be under α-tocopherol-regulation appear rather to be dependent upon the oxidative stress of the cell or tissue under question. Moreover, it seems unlikely that these pathways are specifically under the control of α-tocopherol given that various antioxidants other than α-tocopherol and various oxidative stressors can manipulate their responses. Thus, virtually all of the variation and scope of vitamin E’s biological activity can be seen and understood in the light of protection of polyunsaturated fatty acids and the membrane qualities (fluidity, phase separation and lipid domains) that polyunsaturated fatty acids bring about. Introduction Vitamin E was discovered in 1922 by Evans and Bishop as a necessary dietary factor for reproduction in rats [1]. Subsequent studies showed that the presence of rancid fat in the experimental diets fed to rats and chickens was the causative agent of various pathologies in these animals and that these abnormalities could be “cured” by wheat germ oil concentrates that later were demonstrated to contain tocopherols [2-8], work that has been reviewed by Wolf [9]. Given that most other vitamins have a co-factor function, are ligands for nuclear receptors, or have some unique molecular role; the search for a more specific vitamin E function has continued since its discovery. We propose the hypothesis that all of the observations concerning the in vivo mechanism of action of α-tocopherol result from its role as a lipid soluble antioxidant. Why are the proofs of this hypothesis so scarce after more than 80 years research on vitamin E? If oxidized α-tocopherol accumulated, or even was excreted in detectable amounts, its role as an antioxidant could be readily demonstrated. Instead, the tocopheroxyl radical is formed during the antioxidant action, but then is reduced by other antioxidants and thus the ephemeral oxidation product of α-tocopherol does not remain to be measured. Although this concept of antioxidant interactions has been discussed and demonstrated in vitro [10], it is only recently that evidence has been obtained in humans for its existence [11]. Moreover, a combination deficiency of vitamin E and either selenium [12] or vitamin C [13] results in death to guinea pigs within days of the initiation of the second deficiency. These results highlight the importance of the multiple low molecular weight antioxidant systems necessary for vitamin E’s function. The purpose of this review then is to describe the evidence for α-tocopherol’s in vivo function and to make the claim that α-tocopherol’s vitamin function, if not only function, is that of a peroxyl radical scavenger. The importance of this function is to maintain the integrity of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in the membranes of cells and thus maintain their bioactivity. That is to say that these bioactive lipids are important signaling molecules and that changes in their amounts, or in their loss due to oxidation, or their oxidation products are the key cellular events that are responded to by cells. This hypothesis is supported by studies in plants where the genes for vitamin E synthesis have been knocked out. Sattler et al. [14] show that nonenzymatic lipid peroxidation products in the seedlings from these plants up-regulated genes, and they proposed that increased tocopherol levels in response to environmental stresses may limit nonenzymatic lipid peroxidation and thereby prevent the inappropriate induction of stress responses. Regulation of α-tocopherol concentrations Of the four tocopherols and four tocotrienols (designated as α-, β-, γ-, and δ-) found in food, only α-tocopherol meets human vitamin E requirements [15]. Despite the fact that all of these vitamin Es have similar antioxidant functions (rate constants for H-atom donation within an order of magnitude (Table)), non-α-tocopherols are poorly recognized by the hepatic α-tocopherol transfer protein (α-TTP) [16]. ## Antioxidant mechanisms and biochemical profiles of allium oils versus vitamin E

The evidence suggests that allium oils and vitamin E differ substantially in their major antioxidant compounds, their radical-scavenging mechanisms, and their bioavailability and stability.

### Major antioxidant compounds in allium oils and vitamin E
Allium oils are described as containing organosulfur compounds, which are the proposed biological basis for the antioxidant activity of Allium products [N1-R1]. The evidence also notes that onion oil has been reported to effectively decrease lipid levels in experimental animals, and that onion oil’s biological action is attributed to organosulfur compounds [N1-F1]. For vitamin E, the evidence explicitly identifies α-tocopherol as the principal form studied in vivo, and notes that all naturally occurring vitamin E forms have relatively similar antioxidant properties, with α-tocopherol being the unique form preferred by the body [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that vitamin E includes tocopherols and tocotrienols, with α-tocopherol being the only one meeting human vitamin E requirements [N2-F2].

### How each compound scavenges radicals or inhibits lipid peroxidation
The evidence for allium oils points to a broad antioxidant profile that includes inhibition of lipid peroxidation and scavenging of reactive species. In the nicotine-treated rat study, onion oil was shown to increase resistance to lipid peroxidation and to raise antioxidant defenses, while vitamin E was explicitly compared as a highly efficient antioxidant [N1-F1]. The same study also notes that onion oil supplementation significantly reduced lipid peroxidation products such as TBARS, hydroperoxides, and conjugated dienes, and that the effect was near to that of vitamin E [N1-F1]. For vitamin E, the evidence states that α-tocopherol is proposed as a peroxyl radical scavenger, and that its major function is to maintain the integrity of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes by protecting them from oxidation [N2-F2]. It further notes that vitamin E’s antioxidant action is associated with scavenging peroxyl radicals and with the maintenance of bioactive lipids, which are important signaling molecules [N2-F2].

### Differences in bioavailability, stability, and target pathways
The evidence highlights important differences in stability and targeting. For vitamin E, the evidence notes that α-tocopherol is poorly recognized by the hepatic α-tocopherol transfer protein (α-TTP) compared to other tocopherols, and that defects in α-TTP lead to severe vitamin E deficiency [N2-F2]. This suggests that α-tocopherol has a more restricted bioavailability pathway than other vitamin E forms and that its selective recognition by α-TTP is a key determinant of its tissue distribution. In contrast, the evidence for allium oils is less explicit on bioavailability but emphasizes that organosulfur compounds are the active agents and that onion oil has broad antioxidant effects in tissues exposed to nicotine [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that allium products are organosulfur-based, which implies a different mechanism of action than the lipid-soluble scavenging of α-tocopherol [N1-F1]. Vitamin E’s evidence further indicates that its antioxidant function is not limited to scavenging alone, but is integrated with the regulation of polyunsaturated fatty acid integrity, membrane fluidity, and signaling pathways [N2-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports a distinction between allium oils, which act through organosulfur compounds and broad antioxidant defenses, and vitamin E, which acts primarily as a lipid-soluble peroxyl radical scavenger with a more defined targeting of membrane polyunsaturated fatty acids [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Experimental evidence for allium oils versus vitamin E in nicotine-related oxidative stress

The evidence base for allium oils and vitamin E in nicotine-related oxidative stress is relatively focused, with the most direct comparison coming from studies in nicotine-treated rats. Across these studies, the main outcome is lipid peroxidation, but other oxidative stress endpoints and intervention factors also appear.

### Study outcomes on lipid peroxidation markers in nicotine-exposed rats
The most directly relevant evidence comes from the 2000 study on onion oil versus vitamin E in nicotine-treated rats. In this study, nicotine increased lipid peroxidation products such as TBARS, hydroperoxides, and conjugated dienes in liver, lungs, and heart compared to normal rats [N1-F1]. On onion oil supplementation, lipid peroxide levels were significantly reduced, and the effect was near to that of vitamin E [N1-F1]. The same study also reported that vitamin E supplementation similarly reduced lipid peroxidation products and raised antioxidant defenses [N1-F1]. In the 2020 granulosa-cell study, vitamin E reduced nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation markers such as lipid peroxide (LPO), malondialdehyde (MDA), and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) in granulosa cells, and was associated with reduced apoptosis and improved follicle health [N4-F4]. This indicates that the lipid peroxidation response to nicotine is measurable in multiple tissues and that both allium oils and vitamin E can reduce it.

### Dose-response and intervention timing effects
The studies show dose and timing dependence. In the onion oil/vitamin E study, rats were injected with nicotine (0.6 mg/kg body wt.) and simultaneously given onion oil or vitamin E at 100 mg/kg body wt. for 21 days [N1-F1]. This suggests a chronic intervention protocol. In the granulosa-cell study, nicotine and vitamin E were administered intraperitoneally once daily for 2 weeks, with nicotine at 1 mg/kg/day and vitamin E at 200 mg/kg/day [N4-F4]. The evidence also notes that in the nicotine-related oxidative stress studies, the highest changes in lymphocytes were observed at the dose of 1.0 mg/kg/day for 7 days [N6-R5]. This implies that the magnitude and timing of nicotine exposure can influence the response, and that intervention timing matters for efficacy. However, the evidence provided here does not provide a detailed dose-response curve across multiple doses, so the evidence is descriptive rather than fully quantitative.

### Whether allium oils or vitamin E showed greater protection
The direct comparison in the onion oil/vitamin E study suggests that onion oil and vitamin E had similar protective effects on lipid peroxidation [N1-F1]. The study concluded that onion oil is an effective antioxidant against nicotine-induced oxidative damage as compared to vitamin E [N1-F1]. However, the wording is important: the study says the effect was “near to that of vitamin E fed rats,” and that onion oil “is an effective antioxidant against the oxidative damage caused by nicotine as compared to vitamin E” [N1-F1]. That wording suggests a close similarity rather than a clear superiority of one over the other. The granulosa-cell study provides further evidence that vitamin E reduced lipid peroxidation markers and improved follicular health, but it does not directly compare vitamin E to allium oils [N4-F4]. In contrast, the study on vitamin E in granulosa cells is a more tissue-specific and mechanistic study, while the onion oil study is a broader comparison across tissues [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence base indicates that both allium oils and vitamin E can reduce nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation, but the comparison is limited and the evidence is most consistent with comparable protection rather than one clearly outperforming the other [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## Whether nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation is the main outcome or whether other oxidative stress endpoints are also reported

The evidence indicates that nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation is the main outcome in many of the relevant studies, but other oxidative stress endpoints are also commonly reported. This makes a direct comparison with vitamin E more difficult because the studies may measure different aspects of antioxidant status.

### Which lipid peroxidation markers are measured
The most directly relevant lipid peroxidation markers in the evidence are TBARS, hydroperoxides, conjugated dienes, lipid peroxide, malondialdehyde (MDA), and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE). In the onion oil/vitamin E study, TBARS, hydroperoxides, and conjugated dienes were significantly increased in nicotine-treated rats, and onion oil or vitamin E supplementation reduced these markers [N1-F1]. In the granulosa-cell study, LPO, MDA, and 4-HNE were measured as lipid peroxidation products, and vitamin E reduced them [N4-F4]. The study on ferulic acid and NAC also mentions lipid peroxidation as an outcome, but the relevant excerpt is only partial [N4-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports a standard set of lipid peroxidation endpoints, with MDA and TBARS being the most commonly cited markers.

### Whether studies report other antioxidants or oxidative stress biomarkers
Yes. The studies go beyond lipid peroxidation to report other antioxidants and oxidative stress biomarkers. In the onion oil/vitamin E study, catalase and superoxide dismutase activities decreased in nicotine-treated rats, and antioxidants such as glutathione, vitamin C, and retinol were also measured [N1-F1]. The study also notes that liver vitamin E content decreased in nicotine-treated rats, while vitamin E supplementation increased antioxidant concentrations in tissues [N1-F1]. In the granulosa-cell study, 17-β estradiol (E2), follicle count, and granulosa cell proliferation were measured, along with apoptotic markers such as TUNEL reactivity [N4-F4]. The 2020 study on vitamin E in granulosa cells also reports mitochondrial damage and autophagosomes as ultrastructural endpoints [N4-F4]. The study on ferulic acid and NAC notes circulatory lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase as well as lipid peroxidation [N4-R2]. The nicotine-induced redox imbalance study in rats also reports oxidative stress and antioxidant markers in serum [N5-R1]. So the evidence base is broader than lipid peroxidation alone.

### Whether findings support a direct comparison with vitamin E
The findings do support a direct comparison with vitamin E, but only when the comparison is framed around lipid peroxidation and related antioxidant responses. The onion oil/vitamin E study directly compares the two interventions and reports comparable lipid peroxidation suppression [N1-F1]. The granulosa-cell study provides strong evidence for vitamin E’s efficacy against nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation, but it does not include a direct allium-oil comparator [N4-F4]. The broader evidence also shows that studies often include glutathione, catalase, SOD, vitamin C, retinol, and other markers, which means that conclusions about vitamin E may depend on whether the study is measuring only lipid peroxidation or a broader antioxidant profile [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R1]. In short, the evidence supports a direct comparison with vitamin E on lipid peroxidation, but the wider oxidative stress endpoints make it less straightforward to conclude that lipid peroxidation alone is the only relevant measure [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R1].

## Study design, sample size, and limitations across the evidence base

The evidence base is dominated by rodent studies, with some common animal models and exposure protocols, but the sample sizes, statistical power, and generalizability to human smokers are variable.

### Common animal model and exposure protocols
The evidence most consistently uses rats as the animal model, with several studies explicitly mentioning rat strains or rat tissues [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R1]. The most direct nicotine exposure protocol is repeated dosing in rats, with nicotine administered intraperitoneally or via injection [N1-F1][N4-F4]. One study used rats injected with nicotine (0.6 mg/kg body wt.) and given onion oil or vitamin E simultaneously for 21 days [N1-F1]. Another study used intraperitoneal nicotine administration at 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks [N4-F4]. A third study reports nicotine administration in rats at different doses and times, with changes in lymphocytes observed after 7 days [N6-R5]. The evidence also includes a study on passive smoking in Wistar rats and another on chronic nicotine-containing electronic-cigarette exposure in rats, indicating that exposure protocols are not limited to acute nicotine injection [N5-R3][N5-R4]. This suggests a broad range of nicotine-related protocols, from acute to chronic exposure, but the exact models and endpoints differ.

### Sample size and statistical power
The evidence does not consistently report large sample sizes. In the onion oil/vitamin E study, the sample size is explicitly small: 8 rats per group [N4-F4]. In the nicotine-induced granulosa-cell study, the same small group size is used, with 8 rats per group [N4-F4]. In the study on nicotine and serum antioxidants, the sample size is also small and not fully stated in the excerpt, but the study is described as comparing serum antioxidant profiles in rats [N5-R1]. The evidence does not provide a comprehensive summary of statistical power across studies, so it is reasonable to infer that many of these studies are small and may be underpowered to detect subtle differences. The lack of detailed sample size information in the provided excerpts limits a precise assessment of statistical power.

### Confounding factors and generalizability to human smokers
The evidence base includes several confounding factors. First, the studies are mostly in rats, so extrapolation to human smokers is tentative. Second, the studies often combine nicotine with other variables, such as fat intake, alcohol, or cigarette smoke exposure, which can complicate interpretation [N1-F1]. Third, the studies frequently measure oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation in multiple tissues or organs, which can mask organ-specific effects [N1-F1][N4-F4]. Fourth, the use of repeated dosing and long-term exposure can change the biological response over time, but the evidence does not uniformly control for all confounders [N1-F1][N4-F4]. Finally, the evidence includes studies that measure serum antioxidants, oxidative stress biomarkers, and histological changes, which introduces heterogeneity in outcome interpretation [N5-R1]. 

Because of these factors, the generalizability of the findings to human smokers is limited. The studies are useful for mechanistic insight, but they cannot be taken as definitive evidence of human benefit without further clinical validation [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R1].

The studies point to a **similar protective effect**, with allium oils often appearing comparable to vitamin E rather than clearly superior or inferior [N1-F1][N4-F4]. However, the two agents differ in their **antioxidant compounds, mechanisms of action, bioavailability, and target pathways**, which means the comparison should be interpreted as **mechanistically different rather than merely equal** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence indicates that allium oils are rich in **organosulfur compounds**, which are proposed to underlie their antioxidant and therapeutic activity [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The evidence further proposes that α-tocopherol functions primarily as a **peroxyl radical scavenger** and that its major biological role is to protect long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes from oxidation [N2-F2]. It also notes that vitamin E’s antioxidant action is not limited to scavenging alone, but is integrated with the regulation of membrane integrity, fluidity, and signaling pathways [N2-F2].

### Key difference
The main distinction is that **allium oils act through organosulfur compounds and broad antioxidant defenses**, while **vitamin E acts primarily through lipid-soluble peroxyl radical scavenging with a more defined target on membrane polyunsaturated fatty acids** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 2) What do the experimental studies show about nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation?

### Study outcomes on lipid peroxidation markers
The evidence is strongest for **nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation** as the primary outcome, but the studies also measure multiple markers. In the direct comparison of onion oil and vitamin E in nicotine-treated rats, nicotine increased lipid peroxidation products such as TBARS, hydroperoxides, and conjugated dienes in liver, lungs, and heart compared to normal rats [N1-F1]. So, the lipid peroxidation response to nicotine is measurable in multiple tissues, and both agents can reduce it.

### Dose-response and intervention timing
The evidence shows that **dose and timing matter**. In the onion oil/vitamin E study, rats were injected with nicotine (0.6 mg/kg body wt.) and simultaneously given onion oil or vitamin E at 100 mg/kg body wt. for 21 days [N1-F1]. In the granulosa-cell study, nicotine and vitamin E were administered intraperitoneally once daily for 2 weeks, with nicotine at 1 mg/kg/day and vitamin E at 200 mg/kg/day [N4-F4]. The study concluded that onion oil is an effective antioxidant against nicotine-induced oxidative damage as compared to vitamin E [N1-F1]. The granulosa-cell study supports vitamin E’s efficacy against nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation, but it does not include a direct comparison with allium oils [N4-F4].

### Bottom line on experimental evidence
The evidence supports a **close similarity in protective effects** against nicotine-induced lipid peroxidation, but it does not establish a clear superiority of one agent over the other. The comparison is best described as **allium oils ≈ vitamin E in lipid peroxidation reduction**, with vitamin E showing more tissue-specific mechanistic evidence in granulosa cells [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## 3) Are other oxidative stress endpoints reported alongside lipid peroxidation?
